title: The world's coral reefs are in critical danger
credits: Photos: Shifaaz shamoon, Nathan Dumlao, Anders Marlowe / Unsplash · Map: Natural Earth
lines: Almost all of the world's coral reefs are now at risk of collapse, according to a major new scientific assessment.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature studied one hundred and twenty-seven reef systems, covering about one hundred and eighty-eight thousand square kilometres.
It rated ninety-six percent of them as critically endangered, its highest category of risk.
It warns that nearly all shallow-water reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse by twenty seventy-five.
The biggest threat is heat. Warmer oceans are making coral bleaching more frequent and more intense.
Overfishing is another danger. Losing fish like parrotfish and groupers threatens sixty-three percent of reef ecosystems.
Pollution, coastal building, tourism and stronger storms are adding to the pressure.
The list includes famous reefs: Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in South-East Asia, the Caribbean's Mesoamerican reef, and the Red Sea.
The findings were presented on Thursday, at the UN biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.
Coral reefs cover a tiny part of the ocean floor, but they shelter a huge share of marine life and protect coastlines.
The IUCN's director general says it is still not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover.
